M4 · Numerical Methods for Scattering Problems

Learning goals. After this chapter you should be able to

  • prepare the radial equation for the computer: reduced units, step sizes and matching radii;
  • distinguish local and global errors, and compare the order, cost and stability of the Euler,
    Runge–Kutta and Numerov methods;
  • derive the Numerov method, start it at the origin, and predict its phase error;
  • find bound states by shooting and matching, and label them by counting nodes;
  • integrate coupled equations with closed channels, and recognize and cure the loss of linear
    independence;
  • choose a quadrature rule, and know when the trapezoidal rule is exponentially accurate;
  • propagate wave packets with the split-operator and Crank–Nicolson methods, and build absorbing
    boundaries;
  • resum divergent Born or iteration series with Padé approximants;
  • test a scattering code against information that does not come from the code itself.

Prerequisites: M1 (Riccati and Coulomb
functions) and M2 (Green’s functions and
the Lippmann–Schwinger equation). Chapter 2 uses the methods of this chapter and is a good companion.

Sources: C&H §2.2 (numerical solutions of the radial equation) and §9.5 (solution of the
coupled-channel equations); Thompson (1988) §3.3 (bound states), §5.1 (integration of the radial
equations) and §5.2 (convergence of the iterative method); the FRESCO input manual (QR stabilization
and Padé acceleration); Press et al., Numerical Recipes. Longer derivations are collected in the
section Detailed derivation at the end of the chapter.

How to read this chapter. Every method here is tested in the notebook on a problem with a known
answer, and the numbers quoted come from those tests. The main thread is M4.1–M4.5: the radial
equation, its bound states and its coupled-channel form. M4.6–M4.8 cover tools that later chapters
need (quadrature, time propagation, series resummation), and M4.9 collects the checks that a
scattering code should pass.

M4.1 Preparing the radial equation for the computer

The special functions of M1 solve the radial equation exactly only for a few potentials. Realistic
nuclear potentials, with their diffuse surfaces, spin–orbit terms and couplings, must be handled
numerically. The first step is to write the equation in a form that suits the computer. All radial
problems in these notes are solved in reduced units:

u′′(r)+[k2−l(l+1)r2−U(r)]u(r)=0,U=Vℏ2/2μ,k2=Eℏ2/2μ(fm−2),(M4.1)u''(r) + \Big[k^2 - \frac{l(l+1)}{r^2} - U(r)\Big]u(r) = 0,\qquad U = \frac{V}{\hbar^2/2\mu},\qquad k^2 = \frac{E}{\hbar^2/2\mu}\quad(\text{fm}^{-2}), \tag{M4.1} u′′(r)+[k2−r2l(l+1)​−U(r)]u(r)=0,U=ℏ2/2μV​,k2=ℏ2/2μE​(fm−2),(M4.1)

with the conversion constant

ℏ22μ=(ℏc)22μc2=20.90 MeV fm2μ/u,(M4.2)\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu} = \frac{(\hbar c)^2}{2\mu c^2} = \frac{20.90\ \text{MeV fm}^2}{\mu/\text{u}} , \tag{M4.2} 2μℏ2​=2μc2(ℏc)2​=μ/u20.90 MeV fm2​,(M4.2)

where μ/u\mu/\text{u}μ/u is the reduced mass in atomic mass units; the number is
(197.327 MeV fm)2/(2×931.494 MeV)(197.327\ \text{MeV fm})^2/(2\times931.494\ \text{MeV})(197.327 MeV fm)2/(2×931.494 MeV). In these units every quantity in the equation
is an inverse length squared, and three length scales set the numerical parameters. The first is the
wavelength λ=2π/k\lambda = 2\pi/kλ=2π/k, or rather the local wavelength inside the potential, where
kloc2=k2−Uk_{\rm loc}^2 = k^2 - Ukloc2​=k2−U is larger. For n + ⁴⁰Ca at 10 MeV in a 51 MeV well, λ=9.3\lambda = 9.3λ=9.3 fm outside
but only 3.7 fm inside, and the step hhh must resolve the shorter one. The second is the surface
thickness a≈0.5a \approx 0.5a≈0.5–0.70.70.7 fm, over which the potential changes. The third is the range of the
potential, which fixes the matching radius, together with the turning point for Coulomb problems.

M4.2 From Euler to Runge–Kutta

We start with general-purpose integrators, which work with first-order systems. Writing y=(u,u′)y = (u, u')y=(u,u′)
and w(r)=k2−l(l+1)/r2−U(r)w(r) = k^2 - l(l+1)/r^2 - U(r)w(r)=k2−l(l+1)/r2−U(r), (M4.1) becomes

y′=f(r,y)=(u′, −w(r) u).(M4.3)y' = f(r, y) = \big(u',\ -w(r)\,u\big) . \tag{M4.3} y′=f(r,y)=(u′, −w(r)u).(M4.3)

The simplest method, forward Euler, follows the tangent:

yn+1=yn+h f(rn,yn).(M4.4)y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f(r_n, y_n) . \tag{M4.4} yn+1​=yn​+hf(rn​,yn​).(M4.4)

Comparing with the Taylor series y(rn+h)=yn+hyn′+12h2yn′′+…y(r_n + h) = y_n + hy_n' + \frac12h^2y_n'' + \dotsy(rn​+h)=yn​+hyn′​+21​h2yn′′​+… shows that Euler
drops the term in h2h^2h2: its local error, made in one step, is O(h2)O(h^2)O(h2). Over a fixed distance LLL
the L/hL/hL/h local errors add up to a global error O(h)O(h)O(h), so the method is of first order. In
general, a local error O(hp+1)O(h^{p+1})O(hp+1) gives a global error O(hp)O(h^p)O(hp), provided the errors are not amplified
along the way, a point we return to below. Higher accuracy requires more information about the slope
within each step. The classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method samples it four times:

k1=f(rn,yn),k2=f(rn+h2, yn+h2k1),k3=f(rn+h2, yn+h2k2),k4=f(rn+h, yn+hk3),yn+1=yn+h6 (k1+2k2+2k3+k4),(M4.5)\begin{aligned} &k_1 = f(r_n, y_n),\qquad k_2 = f\big(r_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2k_1\big),\qquad k_3 = f\big(r_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2k_2\big),\qquad k_4 = f(r_n + h,\ y_n + hk_3),\\ &y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac h6\,(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4) , \end{aligned} \tag{M4.5} ​k1​=f(rn​,yn​),k2​=f(rn​+2h​, yn​+2h​k1​),k3​=f(rn​+2h​, yn​+2h​k2​),k4​=f(rn​+h, yn​+hk3​),yn+1​=yn​+6h​(k1​+2k2​+2k3​+k4​),​(M4.5)

with local error O(h5)O(h^5)O(h5) and global error O(h4)O(h^4)O(h4). When fff does not depend on yyy, the weights
16,26+26,16\frac16, \frac26 + \frac26, \frac1661​,62​+62​,61​ are exactly those of Simpson’s rule on one step, whose local error is
also O(h5)O(h^5)O(h5); the nested evaluations extend this accuracy to equations in which the slope depends on
the solution.

To compare methods we need a test with an exact answer, and the exponential well
U=−U0e−r/aU = -U_0e^{-r/a}U=−U0​e−r/a provides one. With x=2aU0 e−r/2ax = 2a\sqrt{U_0}\,e^{-r/2a}x=2aU0​​e−r/2a the s-wave equation becomes Bessel’s
equation of the imaginary order ν=2iak\nu = 2iakν=2iak, and the phase shift follows from Bessel and Gamma
functions of complex argument (derivation D.1; scatlib.phaseshift.exponential_well). For
U0=2U_0 = 2U0​=2 fm⁻², a=1.5a = 1.5a=1.5 fm and k=1k = 1k=1 fm⁻¹, δ0=1.221548891155\delta_0 = 1.221548891155δ0​=1.221548891155. Fig. M4.1a shows the error of
the computed phase shift against hhh. Euler is first order, with fitted order 0.98, and RK4 fourth
order (4.00). To reach 10−610^{-6}10−6 rad, Euler would need about 1.7×1071.7\times10^71.7×107 evaluations of the potential
and RK4 about 4100.

Order is not everything; a method must also be stable. For a free wave the exact solution keeps its
amplitude. One Euler step multiplies the vector (u,u′/k)(u, u'/k)(u,u′/k) by the matrix
(1kh−kh1)\begin{pmatrix}1 & kh\\ -kh & 1\end{pmatrix}(1−kh​kh1​), whose eigenvalues are 1±ikh1 \pm ikh1±ikh, so every step amplifies the
wave by 1+(kh)2\sqrt{1 + (kh)^2}1+(kh)2​. RK4 multiplies each component by R(±ikh)R(\pm ikh)R(±ikh), where
R(z)=1+z+z2/2+z3/6+z4/24R(z) = 1 + z + z^2/2 + z^3/6 + z^4/24R(z)=1+z+z2/2+z3/6+z4/24 is the Taylor polynomial of eze^zez, and ∣R(ikh)∣|R(ikh)|∣R(ikh)∣ falls just short
of 1 (derivation D.2):

∣AEuler∣=[1+(kh)2]1/2,∣ARK4∣=1−(kh)6144+O((kh)8)per step.(M4.6)|A_{\rm Euler}| = \big[1 + (kh)^2\big]^{1/2},\qquad |A_{\rm RK4}| = 1 - \frac{(kh)^6}{144} + O\big((kh)^8\big)\qquad\text{per step}. \tag{M4.6} ∣AEuler​∣=[1+(kh)2]1/2,∣ARK4​∣=1−144(kh)6​+O((kh)8)per step.(M4.6)

After 50 wavelengths at kh=0.2kh = 0.2kh=0.2 the Euler amplitude has grown by a factor 2.4×10132.4\times10^{13}2.4×1013, while
RK4 has lost 7×10−47\times10^{-4}7×10−4 of it (Fig. M4.1b). An unstable method can be first order and still
useless.

M4.3 The Numerov method

The radial equation has two special features that general-purpose methods ignore: it is linear, and it
has no first-derivative term. The Numerov method exploits both. Adding the Taylor expansions of
u(r±h)u(r \pm h)u(r±h) cancels all odd derivatives, and applying the same step to u′′u''u′′ gives a second relation:

un+1−2un+un−1=h2un′′+h412un(4)+O(h6),h2un(4)=un+1′′−2un′′+un−1′′+O(h4).(M4.7)u_{n+1} - 2u_n + u_{n-1} = h^2u_n'' + \frac{h^4}{12}u_n^{(4)} + O(h^6),\qquad h^2u_n^{(4)} = u''_{n+1} - 2u''_n + u''_{n-1} + O(h^4) . \tag{M4.7} un+1​−2un​+un−1​=h2un′′​+12h4​un(4)​+O(h6),h2un(4)​=un+1′′​−2un′′​+un−1′′​+O(h4).(M4.7)

The fourth derivative, which would otherwise limit the accuracy, can now be eliminated. Insert the
second relation into the first and use the differential equation, u′′=−wuu'' = -wuu′′=−wu, at all three points.
Collecting the terms in un+1u_{n+1}un+1​, unu_nun​ and un−1u_{n-1}un−1​ gives the three-term recursion of Chapter 2
(eq. 2.18):

(1+h212wn+1)un+1=2(1−5h212wn)un−(1+h212wn−1)un−1.(M4.8)\Big(1 + \frac{h^2}{12}w_{n+1}\Big)u_{n+1} = 2\Big(1 - \frac{5h^2}{12}w_n\Big)u_n - \Big(1 + \frac{h^2}{12}w_{n-1}\Big)u_{n-1} . \tag{M4.8} (1+12h2​wn+1​)un+1​=2(1−125h2​wn​)un​−(1+12h2​wn−1​)un−1​.(M4.8)

Its local error is O(h6)O(h^6)O(h6) and its global error O(h4)O(h^4)O(h4), the same order as RK4. But it costs one
evaluation of the potential per step instead of four, and its error constant is smaller. Fig. M4.1a
shows Numerov about four times more accurate than RK4 at the same hhh. It reaches 10−610^{-6}10−6 rad with
about 690 evaluations, six times fewer than RK4.

The Numerov recursion also has ideal stability for waves: it neither amplifies nor damps them. For
constant w=k2w = k^2w=k2, try un=einθu_n = e^{in\theta}un​=einθ in (M4.8). Dividing by einθe^{in\theta}einθ leaves
(1+x/12)(eiθ+e−iθ)=2(1−5x/12)(1 + x/12)(e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}) = 2(1 - 5x/12)(1+x/12)(eiθ+e−iθ)=2(1−5x/12), with x=(kh)2x = (kh)^2x=(kh)2, so

cos⁡θ=1−5x/121+x/12,x=(kh)2,θh=knum≈k[1+(kh)4480].(M4.9)\cos\theta = \frac{1 - 5x/12}{1 + x/12},\quad x = (kh)^2,\qquad \frac{\theta}{h} = k_{\rm num} \approx k\Big[1 + \frac{(kh)^4}{480}\Big] . \tag{M4.9} cosθ=1+x/121−5x/12​,x=(kh)2,hθ​=knum​≈k[1+480(kh)4​].(M4.9)

The right side lies between −1-1−1 and 111 as long as x<6x < 6x<6. For kh<6kh < \sqrt6kh<6​, therefore, θ\thetaθ is real
and the numerical wave neither grows nor decays (Fig. M4.1b, where the amplitude stays at 1 to
10−1410^{-14}10−14). The only error in a free region is the slightly wrong wave number knumk_{\rm num}knum​, whose
expansion in powers of khkhkh is worked out in derivation D.2. The notebook confirms (M4.9):
(knum−k)/k=2.084×10−7(k_{\rm num} - k)/k = 2.084\times10^{-7}(knum​−k)/k=2.084×10−7 at kh=0.1kh = 0.1kh=0.1, against (kh)4/480=2.083×10−7(kh)^4/480 = 2.083\times10^{-7}(kh)4/480=2.083×10−7. The
phase error therefore accumulates linearly with distance, kr(kh)4/480kr(kh)^4/480kr(kh)4/480. With 20 points per
wavelength (kh=0.31kh = 0.31kh=0.31) it amounts to 1.3×10−41.3\times10^{-4}1.3×10−4 rad per wavelength, and with 50 points
(kh=0.13kh = 0.13kh=0.13) to 3×10−63\times10^{-6}3×10−6. This is the quantitative form of the rule “λ/20\lambda/20λ/20”. Integrations
over long distances, as in Coulomb problems, need smaller steps.

At the other end, the integration stops at a matching radius, where the solution is matched to free
solutions. This assumes that the potential has ended, and how fast the result converges depends on how
the potential ends. Fig. M4.2a shows this for the same Woods–Saxon well (n + ⁴⁰Ca, k=1k = 1k=1 fm⁻¹) with

M4.4 Shooting and matching for bound states

Scattering states exist at every positive energy; bound states only at special negative ones, which
must be searched for. A bound state, ε=−κ2<0\varepsilon = -\kappa^2 < 0ε=−κ2<0, must be regular at the origin and decay
at infinity. Outside the potential (M4.1) reads u′′=[κ2+l(l+1)/r2] uu'' = [\kappa^2 + l(l+1)/r^2]\,uu′′=[κ2+l(l+1)/r2]u, and its general solution
is

u(r)=A eκr+B e−κr(for l>0: A κr il(κr)+B κr kl(κr)),(M4.13)u(r) = A\,e^{\kappa r} + B\,e^{-\kappa r}\qquad\big(\text{for } l > 0:\ A\,\kappa r\,i_l(\kappa r) + B\,\kappa r\,k_l(\kappa r)\big), \tag{M4.13} u(r)=Aeκr+Be−κr(for l>0: Aκril​(κr)+Bκrkl​(κr)),(M4.13)

with the modified spherical Bessel functions ili_lil​ (growing) and klk_lkl​ (decaying). The regular solution
has A=0A = 0A=0 only at the eigenvalues. Two strategies find them.

The first is shooting. Integrate outward from the origin at a trial energy. Unless the energy is an
eigenvalue, the solution blows up beyond the well, toward +∞+\infty+∞ or −∞-\infty−∞. The sign of the
blow-up changes at every eigenvalue, so bisection on that sign converges to the eigenvalue
(Animation M4.1). Shooting is simple but wasteful: the growing exponential has to be integrated
through the forbidden region, where it swamps everything else.

The second, matching, avoids this. Integrate outward to a matching radius rmr_mrm​ near the surface, and
inward from a large radius, starting with the decaying solution

uin(r)∝κr kl(κr)(r near rmax⁡).(M4.14)u_{\rm in}(r) \propto \kappa r\,k_l(\kappa r)\qquad(r \text{ near } r_{\max}) . \tag{M4.14} uin​(r)∝κrkl​(κr)(r near rmax​).(M4.14)

Inward integration is stable, because the decaying solution grows toward smaller rrr, so it is the
dominant solution in that direction, the same principle as Miller’s algorithm in M1. The two pieces
belong to one eigenfunction when their logarithmic derivatives agree at rmr_mrm​. The difference of
logarithmic derivatives has poles wherever u(rm)=0u(r_m) = 0u(rm​)=0; a smooth equivalent is the mismatch
function

F(E)=sin⁡(θout−θin),θ=arctan⁡u(rm)u′(rm)/q,(M4.15)F(E) = \sin(\theta_{\rm out} - \theta_{\rm in}),\qquad \theta = \arctan\frac{u(r_m)}{u'(r_m)/q} , \tag{M4.15} F(E)=sin(θout​−θin​),θ=arctanu′(rm​)/qu(rm​)​,(M4.15)

with a fixed scale qqq (1 fm⁻¹ in the notebook). The angle θ\thetaθ describes the direction of the vector
(u′/q,u)(u'/q, u)(u′/q,u), which is the same for the two pieces exactly when their logarithmic derivatives agree, so
FFF vanishes exactly at the eigenvalues (Fig. M4.3a) and stays bounded everywhere. A secant or Newton
search on it converges fast.

Both strategies need to know how many levels to look for, and the oscillation theorem provides this.
The nnn-th bound state of a partial wave has n−1n - 1n−1 nodes, and the number of nodes of the regular
solution at energy EEE equals the number of bound states below EEE. The reason is that raising EEE
increases www everywhere, so the solution oscillates faster, its nodes move inward, and a new node
enters from infinity each time EEE passes an eigenvalue. Counting nodes therefore brackets every level,
and bisection on the count cannot miss one. Narrow gaps or nearly degenerate levels, which defeat a
simple scan of F(E)F(E)F(E), are no problem. scatlib.numerov.bound_states works this way. It also counts the
node that may lie beyond the grid, from the analytic continuation (M4.13).

For neutrons in the Woods–Saxon well of ⁴⁰Ca (51 MeV, R=4.34R = 4.34R=4.34 fm, a=0.67a = 0.67a=0.67 fm), the two methods
find the same levels, which agree to 2×10−112\times10^{-11}2×10−11 MeV:

lll levels (MeV)
0 −38.648545-38.648545−38.648545, −15.180102-15.180102−15.180102
1 −28.310197-28.310197−28.310197, −4.356891-4.356891−4.356891
2 −16.955653-16.955653−16.955653

For the exponential well the exact level is the zero of a Bessel function,
J2aκ(2aU0)=0J_{2a\kappa}(2a\sqrt{U_0}) = 0J2aκ​(2aU0​​)=0 (derivation D.1), here ε=−0.190239225650\varepsilon = -0.190239225650ε=−0.190239225650 fm⁻². The Numerov
eigenvalue converges to it as h4h^4h4, with fitted order 4.04 and an error of 2.5×10−102.5\times10^{-10}2.5×10−10 fm⁻² at

In reaction codes the bound states of transfer form factors are usually found the other way round.
The binding energy is fixed at the measured separation energy, and the depth of the potential is
searched instead (Thompson 1988, §3.3.1). The matching condition is the same; only the unknown
changes.

M4.5 Coupled equations: the matrix Numerov method

Coupled channels (Chapter 9) lead to NNN coupled radial equations,

uc′′(r)+∑c′Wcc′(r) uc′(r)=0,Wcc′=[kc2−lc(lc+1)r2]δcc′−Ucc′(r).(M4.16)u_c''(r) + \sum_{c'}W_{cc'}(r)\,u_{c'}(r) = 0,\qquad W_{cc'} = \Big[k_c^2 - \frac{l_c(l_c+1)}{r^2}\Big]\delta_{cc'} - U_{cc'}(r) . \tag{M4.16} uc′′​(r)+c′∑​Wcc′​(r)uc′​(r)=0,Wcc′​=[kc2​−r2lc​(lc​+1)​]δcc′​−Ucc′​(r).(M4.16)

The system still has no first-derivative term, so the Numerov method carries over. There are NNN
independent regular solutions. Starting each as rlc+1r^{l_c+1}rlc​+1 in one channel, we collect them as the columns
of an N×NN\times NN×N matrix u(r)u(r)u(r), which obeys the Numerov recursion (M4.8) with matrices:

Tn+1 un+1=(12−10 Tn) un−Tn−1 un−1,Tn=1+h212Wn.(M4.17)T_{n+1}\,u_{n+1} = (12 - 10\,T_n)\,u_n - T_{n-1}\,u_{n-1},\qquad T_n = 1 + \frac{h^2}{12}W_n . \tag{M4.17} Tn+1​un+1​=(12−10Tn​)un​−Tn−1​un−1​,Tn​=1+12h2​Wn​.(M4.17)

With TnT_nTn​ as defined, 12−10Tn=2(1−5h2Wn/12)12 - 10T_n = 2(1 - 5h^2W_n/12)12−10Tn​=2(1−5h2Wn​/12), so this is (M4.8) term by term; the only new
feature is that the order of the factors matters, and every matrix multiplies uuu from the left.

Outside the potential, each column is matched at two radii to
uc=Ac (incoming)+Bc (outgoing)u_c = A_c\,(\text{incoming}) + B_c\,(\text{outgoing})uc​=Ac​(incoming)+Bc​(outgoing). In open channels these are h^l(−)\hat h_l^{(-)}h^l(−)​ and
h^l(+)\hat h_l^{(+)}h^l(+)​. In closed channels, kc2=−κc2<0k_c^2 = -\kappa_c^2 < 0kc2​=−κc2​<0, they are the growing and decaying
functions of (M4.13). A physical solution is a combination of the columns that has an incoming wave in
one open channel and no growing component in any closed channel, and this selects the open-open block
of BA−1BA^{-1}BA−1 (derivation D.3):

S=− K1/2 (BA−1)open K−1/2,K=diag(kc).(M4.18)S = -\,K^{1/2}\,\big(BA^{-1}\big)_{\rm open}\,K^{-1/2},\qquad K = \mathrm{diag}(k_c) . \tag{M4.18} S=−K1/2(BA−1)open​K−1/2,K=diag(kc​).(M4.18)

The minus sign is the convention u→i2[h^(−)−S h^(+)]u \to \frac i2[\hat h^{(-)} - S\,\hat h^{(+)}]u→2i​[h^(−)−Sh^(+)] of C&H. The factors K±1/2K^{\pm1/2}K±1/2
normalize the channels to unit flux, since a wave of amplitude α\alphaα in channel ccc carries a flux
proportional to kc∣α∣2k_c|\alpha|^2kc​∣α∣2. With them, SSS is unitary and symmetric for real potentials, which is a
strong check (§M4.9). scatlib.coupled implements (M4.16)–(M4.18).

Closed channels bring a numerical problem that a single equation does not have: the loss of linear
independence. In a closed channel the solutions grow like eκre^{\kappa r}eκr. Through the couplings, every
column picks up this growing component. The columns then become nearly parallel, and the physics, which
lives in their differences, is lost to rounding once the matrix is ill-conditioned beyond
1/ϵmachine≈4.5×10151/\epsilon_{\rm machine} \approx 4.5\times10^{15}1/ϵmachine​≈4.5×1015. The notebook tests three channels: two open and one
closed, with κ=1.41\kappa = 1.41κ=1.41 or 3 fm⁻¹, all coupled by a surface form factor with a=0.6a = 0.6a=0.6 fm. With
κ=3\kappa = 3κ=3 fm⁻¹, the condition number of the solution matrix (each channel row normalized) reaches
1/ϵ1/\epsilon1/ϵ near 21 fm. There the unitarity of SSS is lost: ∣SS†−1∣=1.6×10−2|SS^\dagger - 1| = 1.6\times10^{-2}∣SS†−1∣=1.6×10−2 when matched
at 20 fm and 4.3 at 60 fm (Fig. M4.4).

Whether this matters depends on a competition. The open channels are polluted by the closed one only
through the coupling. For a surface form factor, the coupling decays like e−r/ae^{-r/a}e−r/a while the
closed-channel solution grows like eκre^{\kappa r}eκr. Their product, the size of the closed-channel component
fed back into the open channels, and with it the error, therefore grows as

error∝e(κ−1/a) r.(M4.19)\text{error} \propto e^{(\kappa - 1/a)\,r} . \tag{M4.19} error∝e(κ−1/a)r.(M4.19)

The notebook confirms this. For κ<1/a=1.67\kappa < 1/a = 1.67κ<1/a=1.67 fm⁻¹ the plain method stays at 10−910^{-9}10−9, out to
80 fm for κ=1.3\kappa = 1.3κ=1.3 and 1.6 fm⁻¹ and out to 60 fm for κ=1.41\kappa = 1.41κ=1.41 fm⁻¹ (Fig. M4.4). For
κ=1.9\kappa = 1.9κ=1.9 and 2.2 fm⁻¹ the error grows at the rates 0.23 and 0.58 fm⁻¹, against
κ−1/a=0.23\kappa - 1/a = 0.23κ−1/a=0.23 and 0.53 fm⁻¹. Couplings that decay slowly are therefore the most dangerous.
Coulomb couplings fall off only as powers of rrr, which is why continuum-discretized coupled-channel
(CDCC) calculations with closed breakup channels need stabilization.

The cure is re-orthogonalization. Any linear combination of regular solutions is again a regular
solution. Every few steps, we may therefore replace the columns by an orthonormal combination of
themselves. With the QR decomposition un=QRu_n = QRun​=QR, replace

un→unR−1,un−1→un−1R−1,(M4.20)u_n \to u_n R^{-1},\qquad u_{n-1} \to u_{n-1}R^{-1} , \tag{M4.20} un​→un​R−1,un−1​→un−1​R−1,(M4.20)

so that the new un=Qu_n = Qun​=Q has orthonormal columns. Because every matrix in (M4.17) multiplies uuu from
the left, the recursion continues unchanged for u Cu\,CuC with any constant matrix CCC. And the matching
gives ACACAC and BCBCBC instead of AAA and BBB, so BA−1BA^{-1}BA−1, and with it SSS, is unchanged (derivation D.3). The
columns are independent again, and nothing physical has changed. Re-orthogonalizing every 0.5 fm keeps
∣SS†−1∣|SS^\dagger - 1|∣SS†−1∣ at 1.2×10−91.2\times10^{-9}1.2×10−9 for all matching radii, and SSS symmetric to 1.3×10−91.3\times10^{-9}1.3×10−9. FRESCO
does the same: the stabilization of Baylis and Peel (1982) with a QR decomposition, switched on by the
input variable hort (a typical value is 5 fm) and extended by rmort. According to its manual, the
test case dNi-cdcc-QR (d + ⁵⁸Ni at 20 MeV with closed breakup channels) fails without it for total
angular momenta above 3. An alternative family of methods propagates ratios of solutions instead of the
solutions themselves (log-derivative or RRR-matrix propagation, Johnson’s renormalized Numerov), and is
stable by construction.

stays near 10310^3103, for κ=3\kappa = 3κ=3 fm⁻¹ it reaches 1/ϵmachine1/\epsilon_{\rm machine}1/ϵmachine​ near 21 fm.
(b) Unitarity error of the open-channel S-matrix against the matching radius, for the plain method

M4.6 Quadrature

Solving differential equations is only half of the numerical work. Integrals of wave functions (form
factors, the integral formula for sin⁡δ\sin\deltasinδ, DWBA amplitudes) and angular integrals of cross sections
are done by quadrature, ∫abf dx≈∑iwif(xi)\int_a^bf\,dx \approx \sum_iw_if(x_i)∫ab​fdx≈∑i​wi​f(xi​). Three rules cover most needs:

trapezoid: w=h(12,1,…,1,12),Simpson: w=h3(1,4,2,4,…,4,1),Gauss–Legendre: ∫−11P(x) dx=∑i=1NwiP(xi) for deg⁡P≤2N−1.(M4.21)\text{trapezoid: } w = h\big(\tfrac12, 1, \dots, 1, \tfrac12\big),\qquad \text{Simpson: } w = \tfrac h3(1, 4, 2, 4, \dots, 4, 1),\qquad \text{Gauss–Legendre: } \textstyle\int_{-1}^1 P(x)\,dx = \sum_{i=1}^Nw_iP(x_i)\ \text{for}\ \deg P \le 2N - 1 . \tag{M4.21} trapezoid: w=h(21​,1,…,1,21​),Simpson: w=3h​(1,4,2,4,…,4,1),Gauss–Legendre: ∫−11​P(x)dx=∑i=1N​wi​P(xi​) for degP≤2N−1.(M4.21)

The trapezoidal rule replaces fff by straight lines, and Simpson’s rule by parabolas through three
points; their errors fall as h2h^2h2 and h4h^4h4. Gauss–Legendre quadrature instead places its NNN nodes at
the zeros of PNP_NPN​, and that choice doubles the polynomial degree it integrates exactly. To see why,
divide a polynomial PPP of degree ≤2N−1\le 2N - 1≤2N−1 by PNP_NPN​: P=qPN+rP = qP_N + rP=qPN​+r, with qqq and rrr of degree
≤N−1\le N - 1≤N−1. The term qPNqP_NqPN​ integrates to zero by the orthogonality (M1.9) and vanishes at the nodes,
while rrr is integrated exactly by any interpolatory rule with NNN nodes. Hence the rule is exact for PPP,
and for analytic integrands it converges exponentially. Fig. M4.5a confirms these rates for
∫−11dx/(1+25x2)\int_{-1}^1dx/(1 + 25x^2)∫−11​dx/(1+25x2). With 41 points the errors are 3.1×10−53.1\times10^{-5}3.1×10−5, 1.5×10−61.5\times10^{-6}1.5×10−6 and
8.6×10−88.6\times10^{-8}8.6×10−8.

The trapezoidal rule, however, can be spectacular. The Euler–Maclaurin formula gives its error as
a series in powers of hhh (derivation D.4):

Th−∫abf dx=∑j≥1B2j h2j(2j)![f(2j−1)(b)−f(2j−1)(a)],(M4.22)T_h - \int_a^bf\,dx = \sum_{j\ge1}\frac{B_{2j}\,h^{2j}}{(2j)!}\Big[f^{(2j-1)}(b) - f^{(2j-1)}(a)\Big] , \tag{M4.22} Th​−∫ab​fdx=j≥1∑​(2j)!B2j​h2j​[f(2j−1)(b)−f(2j−1)(a)],(M4.22)

with B2jB_{2j}B2j​ the Bernoulli numbers; the first term is h212[f′(b)−f′(a)]\frac{h^2}{12}[f'(b) - f'(a)]12h2​[f′(b)−f′(a)]. Every term involves
only the derivatives at the end points. If all odd derivatives agree at the two ends, every power-law
term cancels, and what remains is exponentially small. That happens for periodic integrands, and for
integrands that decay smoothly to zero at both ends or are even about an end point. In Fourier
language, the trapezoidal sum differs from the integral only by the Fourier transform of fff at the
wave numbers 2πm/h2\pi m/h2πm/h, m≠0m \ne 0m=0, which is exponentially small for a smooth fff (derivation D.4).
Fig. M4.5b shows the effect for ∫08e−r2cos⁡3r dr\int_0^8e^{-r^2}\cos 3r\,dr∫08​e−r2cos3rdr, whose integrand is even about r=0r = 0r=0 and
negligible at r=8r = 8r=8: the trapezoidal rule reaches rounding level with about 22 points, before
Gauss–Legendre. Simpson’s rule is slower, and here it is even worse than the rule it is meant to
improve. The reason is that Simpson’s rule is the combination (4Th−T2h)/3(4T_h - T_{2h})/3(4Th​−T2h​)/3 of two trapezoidal sums.
When the error of ThT_hTh​ is exponentially small, that of T2hT_{2h}T2h​ is exponentially larger, and the
combination inherits it. This is why the trapezoidal rule served so well for the Fourier integrals of
M2 and for the Nyström kernels of §M4.8.

Principal values are computed by subtracting the singularity (M2, eq. M2.40), which leaves a smooth
integrand for any of these rules.

Figure M4.5. Error of three quadrature rules against the number of function values. (a) A smooth
integrand with nearby complex poles: algebraic convergence for the trapezoidal and Simpson rules,
exponential for Gauss–Legendre. (b) A smoothly decaying integrand on a long interval: all rules
converge exponentially, the trapezoidal rule fastest. (Notebook §M4.6.)

M4.7 Time-dependent problems

Wave packets, used in M0 to visualize scattering, require the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The
split-operator method of M0 (eq. M0.22) applies e−iVΔt/2e−iTΔte−iVΔt/2e^{-iV\Delta t/2}e^{-iT\Delta t}e^{-iV\Delta t/2}e−iVΔt/2e−iTΔte−iVΔt/2, with the
kinetic factor computed exactly by FFT. Its error per step is O(Δt3)O(\Delta t^3)O(Δt3), so after a fixed time it is
O(Δt2)O(\Delta t^2)O(Δt2). The Crank–Nicolson method works with a finite-difference Hamiltonian instead. It
averages the forward and backward Euler steps, ψn+1−ψn=−iΔt2H(ψn+1+ψn)\psi_{n+1} - \psi_n = -\frac{i\Delta t}{2}H(\psi_{n+1} + \psi_n)ψn+1​−ψn​=−2iΔt​H(ψn+1​+ψn​),
which gives

(1+iΔt2H)ψn+1=(1−iΔt2H)ψn,Hψj=−ψj+1−2ψj+ψj−1Δx2+Vjψj(ℏ=2m=1).(M4.23)\Big(1 + \frac{i\Delta t}{2}H\Big)\psi_{n+1} = \Big(1 - \frac{i\Delta t}{2}H\Big)\psi_n,\qquad H\psi_j = -\frac{\psi_{j+1} - 2\psi_j + \psi_{j-1}}{\Delta x^2} + V_j\psi_j \quad(\hbar = 2m = 1). \tag{M4.23} (1+2iΔt​H)ψn+1​=(1−2iΔt​H)ψn​,Hψj​=−Δx2ψj+1​−2ψj​+ψj−1​​+Vj​ψj​(ℏ=2m=1).(M4.23)

The propagator (1−iHΔt/2)/(1+iHΔt/2)(1 - iH\Delta t/2)/(1 + iH\Delta t/2)(1−iHΔt/2)/(1+iHΔt/2) multiplies an eigenstate of energy EEE by
(1−iEΔt/2)/(1+iEΔt/2)(1 - iE\Delta t/2)/(1 + iE\Delta t/2)(1−iEΔt/2)/(1+iEΔt/2), a ratio of complex conjugates. Its modulus is exactly 1, so the
propagator is unitary for Hermitian HHH and the method is stable for any Δt\Delta tΔt; and the ratio agrees
with e−iEΔte^{-iE\Delta t}e−iEΔt up to terms of order (EΔt)3(E\Delta t)^3(EΔt)3, so the method is of second order in time. Each step
solves a tridiagonal system, which costs O(N)O(N)O(N) operations. Both methods conserve the norm exactly.

Fig. M4.6a compares them on a coherent state in a harmonic well, whose exact evolution is known. After
one period on 1024 points, the split-operator error falls as Δt2\Delta t^2Δt2 (fitted order 2.00) to
7×10−67\times10^{-6}7×10−6. Crank–Nicolson is also second order but levels off at 7.5×10−47.5\times10^{-4}7.5×10−4. That floor is
the error of the three-point kinetic energy: by Taylor expansion,
(ψj+1−2ψj+ψj−1)/Δx2=ψ′′+Δx212ψ′′′′+…(\psi_{j+1} - 2\psi_j + \psi_{j-1})/\Delta x^2 = \psi'' + \frac{\Delta x^2}{12}\psi'''' + \dots(ψj+1​−2ψj​+ψj−1​)/Δx2=ψ′′+12Δx2​ψ′′′′+…, an error of order
Δx2\Delta x^2Δx2 that the FFT does not have.

On a periodic grid, outgoing waves must be removed before they come back, and this requires an
absorbing boundary. An absorber is an imaginary potential −iW(x)-iW(x)−iW(x), the same object as the absorptive
part of the optical potential (Chapter 7). The multiplicative mask of M0 is one too: multiplying by
m(x)m(x)m(x) every step is the same as e−WΔt=me^{-W\Delta t} = me−WΔt=m, that is W=−ln⁡m/ΔtW = -\ln m/\Delta tW=−lnm/Δt. An absorber can fail in two
ways. If WWW rises steeply on the scale of the wavelength, it reflects, like the potential step of M0. If
it is too weak, waves pass through it. In the WKB picture the local wave number becomes
k2+iW≈k+iW/2k\sqrt{k^2 + iW} \approx k + iW/2kk2+iW​≈k+iW/2k, so the amplitude decays as exp⁡(−∫W dx/2k)\exp(-\int W\,dx/2k)exp(−∫Wdx/2k), and the transmitted
intensity is

T≈exp⁡ ⁣(−1k∫W dx).(M4.24)T \approx \exp\!\Big(-\frac1k\int W\,dx\Big) . \tag{M4.24} T≈exp(−k1​∫Wdx).(M4.24)

Fig. M4.6b shows the fraction not absorbed, R+TR + TR+T, for a quadratic absorber W=W0(x/L)2W = W_0(x/L)^2W=W0​(x/L)2 with
∫W dx=20\int W\,dx = 20∫Wdx=20, computed exactly with the transfer matrices of M0. Reflection dominates at low kkk
and falls as the absorber gets longer. Transmission dominates at high kkk and is the same for all
lengths, as (M4.24) predicts. The window where R+T<10−3R + T < 10^{-3}R+T<10−3 is 0.56<k<2.830.56 < k < 2.830.56<k<2.83 for L=20L = 20L=20, but
only 1.60<k<2.581.60 < k < 2.581.60<k<2.58 for L=5L = 5L=5. An absorber must be several wavelengths long for the slowest
components, and strong enough (∫W dx≫k\int W\,dx \gg k∫Wdx≫k) for the fastest.

step: split-operator (FFT kinetic energy) and Crank–Nicolson (three-point kinetic energy, Δx=0.023\Delta x = 0.023Δx=0.023).
(b) Fraction of a wave not absorbed (reflected plus transmitted) by a quadratic imaginary potential of

M4.8 Summing slowly converging series: Padé approximants

The last tool deals with series that converge slowly or not at all. The Lippmann–Schwinger equation
(M2), ψ=j^l+λG0Uψ\psi = \hat j_l + \lambda G_0U\psiψ=j^​l​+λG0​Uψ for the potential λU\lambda UλU, can be solved by iteration, inserting the
right side into itself again and again. This generates the Born series, and the amplitude
T=eiδsin⁡δT = e^{i\delta}\sin\deltaT=eiδsinδ becomes a power series in the strength λ\lambdaλ:

T(λ)=∑n≥1tnλn,convergent if and only if ∣λ ηi∣<1 for all i,(M4.25)T(\lambda) = \sum_{n\ge1}t_n\lambda^n,\qquad \text{convergent if and only if } |\lambda\,\eta_i| < 1 \text{ for all } i , \tag{M4.25} T(λ)=n≥1∑​tn​λn,convergent if and only if ∣ληi​∣<1 for all i,(M4.25)

where the ηi\eta_iηi​ are the Weinberg eigenvalues, the eigenvalues of the kernel G0UG_0UG0​U. The criterion is
that of a geometric series. Expanded in the eigenvectors of G0UG_0UG0​U, each component of the iterated
solution is multiplied by ληi\lambda\eta_iληi​ in every iteration, so the series converges only if every
∣ληi∣|\lambda\eta_i|∣ληi​∣ is below 1 (derivation D.5). An attractive potential strong enough to bind has
∣η1∣>1|\eta_1| > 1∣η1​∣>1 at low energy, so its Born series diverges at the physical strength λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1. The same
happens to the iterative solution of coupled-channel equations when the couplings are strong. Each
iteration adds one more order of the coupling (Thompson 1988, §5.2).

A divergent series still contains the information needed to compute its sum, if it is used
differently. The [L/M][L/M][L/M] Padé approximant is the rational function that agrees with the series up to
the order L+ML + ML+M:

[L/M] (λ)=p0+p1λ+⋯+pLλL1+q1λ+⋯+qMλM,[L/M] (λ)−T(λ)=O(λL+M+1).(M4.26)[L/M]\,(\lambda) = \frac{p_0 + p_1\lambda + \dots + p_L\lambda^L}{1 + q_1\lambda + \dots + q_M\lambda^M},\qquad [L/M]\,(\lambda) - T(\lambda) = O(\lambda^{L+M+1}) . \tag{M4.26} [L/M](λ)=1+q1​λ+⋯+qM​λMp0​+p1​λ+⋯+pL​λL​,[L/M](λ)−T(λ)=O(λL+M+1).(M4.26)

Multiplying the second condition by the denominator and comparing powers of λ\lambdaλ gives linear
equations, first for the qjq_jqj​ (from the powers L+1,…,L+ML + 1, \dots, L + ML+1,…,L+M, where the numerator contributes
nothing), then for the pkp_kpk​:

∑j=0Mqj ck−j=0(k=L+1,…,L+M, q0=1),pk=∑j=0min⁡(k,M)qj ck−j(k=0,…,L),(M4.27)\sum_{j=0}^{M}q_j\,c_{k-j} = 0\quad(k = L+1, \dots, L+M,\ q_0 = 1),\qquad p_k = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,M)}q_j\,c_{k-j}\quad(k = 0, \dots, L) , \tag{M4.27} j=0∑M​qj​ck−j​=0(k=L+1,…,L+M, q0​=1),pk​=j=0∑min(k,M)​qj​ck−j​(k=0,…,L),(M4.27)

where the ckc_kck​ are the series coefficients. The system becomes ill-conditioned when the ckc_kck​ grow
fast; rescaling λ\lambdaλ by the radius of convergence helps. The same diagonal approximants can be
computed from the partial sums sns_nsn​ alone, without solving equations, by Wynn’s ε algorithm:

ε−1(n)=0,ε0(n)=sn,εk+1(n)=εk−1(n+1)+1εk(n+1)−εk(n),(M4.28)\varepsilon^{(n)}_{-1} = 0,\qquad \varepsilon^{(n)}_0 = s_n,\qquad \varepsilon^{(n)}_{k+1} = \varepsilon^{(n+1)}_{k-1} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{(n+1)}_k - \varepsilon^{(n)}_k} , \tag{M4.28} ε−1(n)​=0,ε0(n)​=sn​,εk+1(n)​=εk−1(n+1)​+εk(n+1)​−εk(n)​1​,(M4.28)

whose even columns are Padé approximants, ε2k(n)=[n+k/k]\varepsilon^{(n)}_{2k} = [n+k/k]ε2k(n)​=[n+k/k]. FRESCO offers both options: its
input variable PADE = 1 uses the ε algorithm, and PADE = 2 the explicit N/DN/DN/D polynomials, to
accelerate or resum the iterations of coupled-channel equations.

Padé approximants work because of the analytic structure of the amplitude. The exact amplitude is

T(λ)=−λk ⟨j^l∣ U (1−λG0U)−1∣j^l⟩,(M4.29)T(\lambda) = -\frac{\lambda}{k}\,\big\langle\hat j_l\big|\,U\,(1 - \lambda G_0U)^{-1}\big|\hat j_l\big\rangle , \tag{M4.29} T(λ)=−kλ​⟨j^​l​∣∣∣​U(1−λG0​U)−1∣∣∣​j^​l​⟩,(M4.29)

and the same eigenvector expansion shows that it is a meromorphic function of λ\lambdaλ, a sum of simple
poles at λ=1/ηi\lambda = 1/\eta_iλ=1/ηi​ (derivation D.5). A power series cannot reach past its nearest pole, whereas a
rational function can represent the poles themselves.

The notebook takes a Woods–Saxon well with U0=0.4U_0 = 0.4U0​=0.4 fm⁻² (about 8 MeV for a nucleon), R=4R = 4R=4 fm,
a=0.6a = 0.6a=0.6 fm, and k=0.4k = 0.4k=0.4 fm⁻¹. The largest Weinberg eigenvalue has ∣η1∣=1.88|\eta_1| = 1.88∣η1​∣=1.88, so the series
converges only for ∣λ∣<0.53|\lambda| < 0.53∣λ∣<0.53. At λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1, where the well holds one bound state, the
partial sums diverge: their error is 7×1087\times10^87×108 after 32 terms. The Padé approximant [7/7][7/7][7/7], built
from 14 terms of the same diverging series, gives TTT to 3×10−133\times10^{-13}3×10−13, and the ε algorithm gives the
same (Fig. M4.7a). The poles of [6/6][6/6][6/6] reproduce the two singularities nearest the origin,
1/η=0.0851−0.5246i1/\eta = 0.0851 - 0.5246i1/η=0.0851−0.5246i and 2.6121−0.9359i2.6121 - 0.9359i2.6121−0.9359i, to all four digits printed (Fig. M4.7b). The nearest
singularity lies off the real axis. Nothing visible happens on the real λ\lambdaλ axis at the radius of
convergence (Animation M4.2), yet that complex pole alone makes the series diverge beyond it. At high
orders, rounding produces spurious pole–zero pairs (Froissart doublets). They cancel in the value of the
approximant, but they are a reason not to push the order further than needed.

M4.9 How to test a scattering code

All the methods of this chapter end up in code, and a scattering code produces numbers that look
plausible whether they are right or wrong. It must therefore be tested against information that does
not come from the code itself. The notebook runs such a battery on scatlib:

matching radius: δ(15 fm)−δ(30 fm)\delta(15\ \text{fm}) - \delta(30\ \text{fm})δ(15 fm)−δ(30 fm), Woods–Saxon 6.8×10−86.8\times10^{-8}6.8×10−8 rad 10−610^{-6}10−6
absorption: max⁡∣Sl∣≤1\max\lvert S_l\rvert \le 1max∣Sl​∣≤1 with an imaginary potential holds —
optical theorem: σel+σR\sigma_{\rm el} + \sigma_Rσel​+σR​ against (4π/k) Im f(0)(4\pi/k)\,\mathrm{Im}\,f(0)(4π/k)Imf(0) from the summed amplitude 7×10−167\times10^{-16}7×10−16 10−1210^{-12}10−12
σel\sigma_{\rm el}σel​ from ∫∣f∣2dΩ\int\lvert f\rvert^2d\Omega∫∣f∣2dΩ (Gauss–Legendre) against the partial-wave sum 2.1×10−142.1\times10^{-14}2.1×10−14 10−1010^{-10}10−10

The general recipe has five parts, and the table draws on all of them. The first is exactly solvable
models for each piece: the hard sphere, the square well, the exponential well, Coulomb scattering and
free motion in coupled channels. The second is convergence: in the step size, at the expected order,
and in the matching radius, the number of partial waves and the number of channels. The third is
conservation laws and symmetries: unitarity and the optical theorem, ∣S∣≤1|S| \le 1∣S∣≤1 with absorption,
S=STS = S^TS=ST by time reversal, and independence of the coupling order (M3). The fourth is theorems, such
as Levinson’s theorem, Wronskian identities and threshold laws. The fifth is other codes: the
benchmarks against FRESCO and CCFULL in Chapters 6–14. A code that passes all of these can still be
applied to the wrong physics, but it is unlikely to compute the right physics wrongly.

Summary

Numerical work on the radial equation starts with reduced units, U=V/(ℏ2/2μ)U = V/(\hbar^2/2\mu)U=V/(ℏ2/2μ) with
ℏ2/2μ=20.90/μ[u]\hbar^2/2\mu = 20.90/\mu[\text{u}]ℏ2/2μ=20.90/μ[u] MeV fm², a step that resolves both the local wavelength and the surface,
and a matching radius beyond the potential. A method with local error O(hp+1)O(h^{p+1})O(hp+1) has global error
O(hp)O(h^p)O(hp) only if it is stable: Euler is first order and amplifies waves without bound, RK4 is fourth
order with a slight damping, and Numerov, which uses the linearity and the missing first derivative of
the radial equation, is fourth order with a single potential evaluation per step, conserves the
amplitude exactly and has only the phase error kr(kh)4/480kr(kh)^4/480kr(kh)4/480. How fast the matching radius converges
depends on how the potential ends: exponential tails converge quickly, power-law tails are better
corrected analytically with the Born estimate, and Coulomb problems must be matched to Coulomb
functions. Bound states are found by shooting or, more robustly, by matching outward and inward
solutions, with node counting to label and bracket every level. Coupled equations with closed channels
lose linear independence when the closed-channel solution grows faster than the coupling decays, and
re-orthogonalization by QR, as in FRESCO, restores it at no physical cost because the S-matrix is
invariant under any recombination of the solutions. Among quadrature rules, Gauss–Legendre converges
exponentially for analytic integrands, while the trapezoidal rule does so for smooth decaying or
periodic ones, because its Euler–Maclaurin error terms cancel. Split-operator and Crank–Nicolson
propagation are unitary and second order in time, and absorbing boundaries are imaginary potentials
that must be long enough to avoid reflection and strong enough to stop transmission. Finally, divergent
Born or iteration series can be resummed by Padé approximants, computed from the coefficients or by
Wynn’s ε algorithm; they succeed because the amplitude is a meromorphic function of the coupling
strength, with poles at the inverse Weinberg eigenvalues.

D.3 The multichannel S-matrix and its invariance

Outside the potential, every column of the solution matrix is a combination of the incoming and
outgoing functions of each channel. Collect these functions in the diagonal matrices
H(∓)(r)=diag(hc(∓)(r))H^{(\mp)}(r) = \mathrm{diag}\big(h_c^{(\mp)}(r)\big)H(∓)(r)=diag(hc(∓)​(r)), with hc(−)=h^lc(−)(kcr)h_c^{(-)} = \hat h^{(-)}_{l_c}(k_cr)hc(−)​=h^lc​(−)​(kc​r) and
hc(+)=h^lc(+)(kcr)h_c^{(+)} = \hat h^{(+)}_{l_c}(k_cr)hc(+)​=h^lc​(+)​(kc​r) in open channels, and the growing and decaying functions (M4.13) in
closed channels. Then

u(r)=H(−)(r) A+H(+)(r) B,u(r) = H^{(-)}(r)\,A + H^{(+)}(r)\,B , u(r)=H(−)(r)A+H(+)(r)B,

and evaluating this at two radii gives two matrix equations from which AAA and BBB follow. A physical
solution is a combination u cu\,cuc of the columns, with a vector ccc of coefficients. It must have unit

D.4 The error of the trapezoidal rule

Consider a single interval [0,h][0, h][0,h]. Integrating by parts with the factor x−h/2x - h/2x−h/2, whose derivative is 1,
